chunks.text: The African oil palm is a single-stemmed, monocotyledonous palm native to a belt of West and southwest Africa stretching from Angola to the Gambia — the species name guineensis refers to the historical region of Guinea along that coast, not the present-day country. Mature palms reach about 20 metres, with pinnate leaves 3–5 metres long; young palms can produce around 30 new leaves a year, settling to about 20 once established past a decade. Its reddish fruit, roughly the size of a large plum, matures over five to six months and grows in large, heavy bunches (5–30 kg depending on the palm's age), each fruit yielding oil from both its fleshy outer pericarp (palm oil) and its single kernel (palm-kernel oil) — the basis of its status as the principal source of palm oil worldwide and, by land-area efficiency, a dramatically higher-yielding oil crop than soy or rapeseed. The species was domesticated in West Africa in antiquity, though exactly when remains undocumented; French naturalist Michel Adanson was the first European to formally describe it and bring seed material back from the region, and the Dutch subsequently introduced it to Java in 1848, with British planters bringing it to Malaysia around 1910 — the beginning of the Southeast Asian plantation industry that now dominates global production, led by Indonesia and Malaysia. The crop's rapid global expansion has made it deeply controversial: while it brings real income, employment and infrastructure to smallholders and national economies, large-scale cultivation is strongly linked to tropical deforestation, biodiversity loss (including of critically endangered species), destructive draining of carbon-rich peat bogs, land-clearing fires that cause regional haze across Southeast Asia, and pollution from untreated palm oil mill effluent — an environmental cost that sits uneasily alongside the crop's unmatched land-use efficiency.

chunks.source: PROTA (Plant Resources of Tropical Africa) — Elaeis guineensis
chunks.text: PROTA's species account goes well beyond the oil-and-deforestation narrative to catalogue just how many products come from a single oil palm. Palm oil (from the fruit's mesocarp) dominates by roughly a 9:1 ratio over palm-kernel oil (from the seed), and in West Africa unrefined red palm oil remains a genuine dietary staple rather than just an export commodity, used directly in cooking alongside margarine, shortenings, snacks and confectionery; about a tenth of palm oil output instead goes into industrial applications such as soap, detergents, candles, cosmetics, lubricating greases and even steel tin-plating, with epoxidised palm oil serving as a PVC plasticiser. Palm-kernel oil, chemically similar to coconut oil, feeds into high-quality soaps and surfactant, plastic and lubricant feedstocks, while the leftover kernel presscake becomes a protein-rich livestock feed. Little is wasted: empty fruit bunches, fibre and shells are burned as boiler or blacksmith fuel or composted into organic fertiliser, palm wine is tapped straight from the inflorescences, the palm heart is eaten as a vegetable, and leaflets, midribs and rachises are woven or built into baskets, brooms and fencing. Traditional medicine across its native range uses palm-heart preparations for gonorrhoea and menorrhagia, leaf sap for skin conditions, and root preparations as an analgesic. Ecologically, PROTA describes it as a light-demanding species of humid tropical lowlands that establishes most readily at swamp edges and along riverbanks, tolerating acidic soils (pH 4.2–5.5) and brief flooding but not permanent waterlogging, and needing consistently high rainfall, humidity and sunshine hours to crop well — explaining why yields in well-managed Southeast Asian plantations (5.2–7.1 tonnes of oil per hectare) so far outstrip the African smallholder average (as low as 0.3 t/ha in Nigeria), even though the species originated in Africa.
